question: How can a funerary object connect royal power, work and belief?
summary: Taharqo’s royal institutions joined temple building and service with skilled production and claims over people and materials. A granite shabti attributed to his reign, probably from Nuri, connects that practical work with elite expectations of labor after death. Royal inscriptions, excavated faience production and a museum object label explain different parts of the history.

sections.title: A kingdom supported through temples
sections.text: Taharqo ruled Egypt and Kush in the Nile valley, with his reign conventionally dated to about 690–664 BCE. At Kawa, in present-day Sudan, he commissioned a sandstone temple and a shrine for Amun. The shrine’s reliefs showed him presenting offerings and wearing royal headgear. The Ashmolean’s teaching account describes priests caring for the god’s statue: awakening it, clothing it and presenting food. A temple therefore connected royal display with repeated practical tasks. People had to supply materials, make and maintain sacred objects, and perform ceremonies. These activities helped present the king’s relationship with Amun as a source of legitimate power.

sections.title: Organising people and skilled work
sections.text: Kawa’s inscriptions also make claims about how the work was organised. In a passage discussed by Aleksandra Hallmann, Taharqo says that he sent work crews, craftspeople and a construction overseer while he remained in Memphis. This is a king announcing his provision, rather than a surviving diary kept by the builders. Another temple inscription lists male and female servants among his gifts. Such wording places people within royal resource claims and makes compulsion a necessary question; it does not tell us every worker’s status, payment or experience.

citations.locator: Hallmann, printed pp. 132–133 / PDF pp. 163–164; Kawa IV lines 21–22 and Kawa III line 22 as discussed there

sections.title: A workshop makes the connection tangible
sections.text: Excavations at another temple founded by Taharqo, Sanam, uncovered firing pits, mudbrick basins, beads and damaged products from making faience, a manufactured quartz-rich material with a glazed surface. A clay mould from inside the temple matches an uninscribed green faience shabti fragment from the workshop. The excavators interpret this seventh-century production as evidence that temple institutions helped organise goods for royal funerary use. It brings skilled making into the explanation of power. This faience evidence concerns a different material and archaeological context from the granite figure shown here; it does not locate this particular figure’s workshop.

sections.title: Work imagined beyond life
sections.text: The selected figure is the Met’s granite shabti of Taharqo, only 20.3 centimetres high, probably associated with his pyramid at Nuri. Shabtis were intended to answer demands for work after death. The Met’s separate Seti I example explains tasks such as cultivation, irrigation and moving sand. That earlier object supplies general context, not a translation of Taharqo’s inscription. Here, a named king was commemorated through an object concerned with service and labor. Its material, carved writing and royal identity connect skilled production with elite expectations of the afterlife, while leaving ordinary households’ beliefs outside what this object alone can establish.

deeperReading.title: Old words can be a deliberate choice
deeperReading.text: A second Taharqo shabti in the British Museum, EA55483, is calcite and has a recorded Nuri findspot. Its catalogue explains that its spell uses fuller, older wording instead of the shortened versions then common. An older model does not automatically make the object older, and borrowing an old text is not evidence that a figure was made after the king died. This comparison shows why material, wording, attributed production date and findspot should be investigated separately. It does not supply a transcription of the Met’s granite figure.

deeperReading.title: Images claim a place in political history
deeperReading.text: Hallmann examines Kawa scenes in which the king appears as a sphinx overcoming enemies. She argues that their artists used older Egyptian compositions but changed the clothing of the depicted Libyan families to make a contemporary political statement. The reliefs consequently give evidence for the way kingship was presented; they need comparison with other sources before describing a particular battle. Read this interpretation alongside the king’s account of crews and temple gifts: both made resources and people visible through a royal voice. They support a history of institutions while leaving the workers’ own accounts largely unheard.

deeperReading.title: Keep the object’s open questions open
deeperReading.text: The consulted sources do not establish later manufacture or reuse of accession 18.2.10. Its reign attribution and probable Nuri origin remain qualified catalogue statements. Further research into the inscription or a secure excavation context could refine either. A shared royal name alone cannot settle when an object was made or how it was used.

evidenceReading.title: Follow a claim from royal words to excavated work
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of the consulted sources, not translations of the displayed figure or quotations from ancient inscriptions.

items.label: A king says that he provided workers
items.text: Hallmann discusses Kawa IV lines 21–22, in which Taharqo claims to have sent work crews, craftspeople and an overseer while he remained in Memphis. She also discusses Kawa III line 22, which lists male and female servants among temple gifts.
items.interpretation: The passages make organised work and claims over people part of royal presentation. They do not give a numerical workforce or establish that every worker shared one legal status, received payment or chose the work. The ancient wording is reached through Hallmann’s discussion following a published translation, not a fresh translation here.

citations.locator: Printed pp. 132–133 / PDF pp. 163–164; Kawa IV lines 21–22 and Kawa III line 22 through Hallmann

items.label: A mould match supports manufacture
items.text: The Sanam excavators report a clay mould from inside the temple matching an uninscribed green faience shabti fragment found in the workshop. Firing pits, basins and production debris supply the wider excavated context.
items.interpretation: Together these observations support making faience objects near the temple; the authors argue that institutions organised royal funerary production. A similar function does not make faience and granite the same material, identify the Met figure’s workshop or turn the broad ceramic chronology into one exact production year.

items.label: A qualified label changes the comparison
items.text: The Met identifies accession 18.2.10 as a granite shabti of Taharqo, attributed to 690–664 BCE and probably associated with Nuri. The British Museum’s separate calcite example EA55483 has a recorded Nuri excavation and uses older spell wording.
items.interpretation: Findspot confidence, attributed date, material and textual model are separate evidence. An older text is not proof of an older or later physical object. The comparison establishes neither a later manufacture date nor a history of reuse for the selected figure.

familyActivity.title: Who made the king’s power visible?
steps: Look at the granite figure. Find two details that required skilled making, and describe what you can see before interpreting their purpose.
Use the source capsule to match three questions to evidence: Who claimed to organise building work? Where is there excavated manufacturing evidence? How certain is this granite figure’s findspot?
Compare the materials named in the object captions: granite, clay and faience. Explain why a mould matching a faience fragment does not locate the granite figure’s workshop.
Choose one further source you would want before describing an individual worker’s life. Explain which unanswered question it could address.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: Hallmann reports Taharqo’s royal claim to send crews and craftspeople to Kawa. At Sanam, excavated firing pits and a clay mould matching an uninscribed faience fragment support manufacture; the authors interpret temple organisation. The Met’s granite shabti is attributed to his reign and probably to Nuri. Carved writing, headgear and crossed hands are visible details; the photograph supplies no translation. Royal claims, excavated production and a probable museum attribution answer different questions.

review.scope: Bounded main, deeper reading, consequential evidence interpretation, supplied family source capsule and distinct phased reference. Complete original interval, stable identity fields, coordinates, packs, original object IDs, claims and existing dimensions preserved. Existing Met catalogue sources renewed only within actually read scopes.
limitations: Selected Hallmann chapter passages and museum teaching/catalogue scopes only; underlying Macadam/Ritner editions, original experiments, chemical analyses and older excavation records not independently consulted. British Museum details were available through its indexed record; direct page access returned 403.

The Sanam publication’s mid-seventh-century abstract and broader ceramic discussion are retained as source conventions, not one exact workshop year or proof of manufacture wholly within/after Taharqo’s reign. Faience evidence does not locate the selected granite figure’s workshop.

No evidence in the consulted scope establishes later manufacture/reuse of Met 18.2.10, an exact excavated findspot, its maker, every worker’s status or universal household belief. These remain questions for further inscription, excavation and social-history research.

placeStudy.title: Nuri and Sanam: burial and production evidence
placeStudy.description: Two published property references near the Fourth Cataract orient different evidence. A probable association of the Met figure with Nuri is not converted into an exact grave findspot. Sanam’s excavated workshop has a broader chronology. Kawa’s building account concerns another place outside this local window; no connecting route or ancient Nile geometry is drawn.
